method: The planned start and the partition size are read in MiB with up to six decimals (decimal comma accepted) and converted to whole bytes by rounding to the nearest byte; the start must be 0 to 1,000,000 MiB and the size 0.000001 to 1,000,000 MiB. The logical and physical sector sizes are limited to 512 and 4096 bytes. The alignment unit is 1 MiB on its own; when a RAID stripe is enabled it becomes the least common multiple of 1 MiB and chunk x data disks, so a 256 KiB chunk over 6 data disks (a 1.5 MiB stripe) needs a 3 MiB unit, and a unit above 1 GiB is refused. The aligned start is the first multiple of the unit at or after the planned start, computed as byte arithmetic with no division; the aligned end is the first multiple at or after start plus size, so the next partition also begins on a boundary. All byte offsets are safe integers, and the start and end LBA are the offsets divided by the logical sector size. The verdict reports a start that is not a whole logical sector, a start that is sector-aligned but not aligned to the physical sector (a 512e drive would read-modify-write), a start that needs padding, or a start that is already aligned. The reference table lists the unit required by five common chunk and disk layouts. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: GNU Parted manual: modern partitioning tools default to an optimal MiB alignment for msdos and gpt labels and can warn when a partition start or end is not aligned.
mdadm(8): the chunk size and the number of data disks define the stripe width that RAID0, RAID5, RAID6 and RAID10 write as one unit.
Linux kernel block-layer documentation: a drive reports both a logical and a physical block size, and requests that do not cover whole physical sectors force read-modify-write on 512e media.
